sources.citation: Rodakowski J, Rocco PB, Ortiz M, Folb B, Schulz R, Morton SC, et al. Caregiver integration during discharge planning for older adults to reduce resource use: a metaanalysis. J Am Geriatr Soc. 2017;65(8):1748-55.
sources.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
sources.population_setting: Older adults (mean age >70) with informal caregivers discharged from hospital or skilled nursing facility to the community; 15 RCTs, 13 unique populations, 4361 patients; 7 US, 8 non-US
sources.correction_check: PubMed record shows no linked erratum or retraction notice (Scite not used).
sources.quality_note: Pooled RRs from 6 (90-day) and 5 (180-day) trials; multicomponent interventions, carer component cannot be isolated; many trials unclear on allocation concealment and blinding; arm-level absolute rates only in figures, not available in the text retrieved; no 30-day pooled result.

sources.citation: Livingston G, Manela M, O'Keeffe A, Rapaport P, Cooper C, Knapp M, et al. Clinical effectiveness of the START (STrAtegies for RelaTives) psychological intervention for family carers and the effects on the cost of care for people with dementia: 6-year follow-up of a randomised controlled trial. Br J Psychiatry. 2020;216(1):35-42.
sources.population_setting: 260 self-identified family carers of people with dementia, London area, UK; randomised 2:1 START vs usual care
sources.correction_check: PubMed record shows no linked erratum or retraction.
sources.quality_note: Care home admission was a secondary outcome; 85.4% included in 6-year analysis.

sources.citation: Mittelman MS, Haley WE, Clay OJ, Roth DL. Improving caregiver well-being delays nursing home placement of patients with Alzheimer disease. Neurology. 2006;67(9):1592-9.
sources.population_setting: 406 spouse caregivers of community-dwelling people with Alzheimer disease, New York, enrolled over 9.5 years
sources.correction_check: PubMed record shows no linked erratum or retraction.
sources.quality_note: 557 days is a model-predicted difference in median time, covariate adjusted; volunteer sample; older era.

sources.citation: Wilson LS, Pillay D, Kelly BD, Casey P. Mental health professionals and information sharing: carer perspectives. Ir J Med Sci. 2015;184(4):781-90.
sources.population_setting: 159 carers of people with mental illness affiliated with a support group, Ireland
sources.correction_check: PubMed record shows no linked erratum or retraction.
sources.quality_note: Small self-selected sample; mental health not geriatric care; Ireland.

claims.claim: In a meta-analysis of randomised trials, discharge planning that integrated family carers was linked with fewer readmissions at 90 and 180 days.
claims.supporting_passage: Discharge planning interventions with caregiver integration were associated with a 25% fewer readmissions at 90 days (relative risk (RR) = 0.75, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.62-0.91) and 24% fewer readmissions at 180 days (RR = 0.76, 95% CI = 0.64-0.90).
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with informal caregivers discharged to community / multicomponent discharge planning including the carer, begun before discharge / usual care / readmission / 90 and 180 days
claims.safe_wording: A review of randomised trials found that discharge plans that brought family carers in were linked with about a quarter fewer readmissions over the next 3 to 6 months (a relative reduction).
claims.qualifications: Relative, not absolute; interventions were multicomponent so the carer part cannot be isolated; pooled from 6 and 5 trials; trial quality often unclear.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Absolute rates not available in text retrieved, so no 'N in 100' statement. No pooled 30-day result. Cochrane review of discharge planning generally (PMID 35199849, other batch) found a smaller relative reduction (RR 0.89) in readmission at about 3 months.

numbers.meaning: relative risk of readmission at 90 days, 6 trials

claims.claim: Common components included written care plans, demonstration of care tasks and teach-back.
claims.supporting_passage: Of the 15 studies, 13 had an intervention component that linked caregivers to external or community resources ... and nine included written care plans. Caregiver assessment was a component in eight studies ... Live or video demonstrations of care tasks was included in five studies, and seven included so-called "teach back" techniques
claims.safe_wording: The programmes that were tested often included a written care plan, linking carers to community services, and showing the carer how to do care tasks and having them show it back.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Authors state it is not possible to determine the most effective method of caregiver integration.

claims.claim: NICE NG150 and the Carers (Scotland) Act require or recommend carer involvement in discharge.
START, an eight-session coping programme for family carers of people with dementia, improved carers' anxiety and depression over six years.
claims.supporting_passage: A total of 260 self-identified family carers of people with dementia were randomised 2:1 to START, an eight-session manual-based coping intervention delivered by supervised psychology graduates, or to treatment as usual (TAU). ... Over 72 months, compared with TAU, the intervention group had improved scores on HADS-T (adjusted mean difference -2.00 points, 95% CI -3.38 to -0.63).
claims.pico_timeframe: UK family carers of people with dementia / START / usual care / HADS total / 72 months
claims.safe_wording: In a UK trial of 260 family carers, an eight-session coping programme left carers with fewer symptoms of anxiety and depression than usual care, and the benefit lasted six years. The average difference was modest.
claims.qualifications: Average difference of 2 points on a 42-point scale; no MCID source verified, so describe as modest, not as clinically large.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Minimal clinically important difference for HADS total not verified.

numbers.meaning: adjusted mean HADS-T difference over 72 months

claims.claim: START did not show a clear difference in time to care home admission.
claims.supporting_passage: Patient-related costs ... and carer-related costs ... were not significantly different between groups nor were group differences in time until care home (intensity ratio START:TAU was 0.88, 95% CI 0.58-1.35).
claims.safe_wording: It did not show a clear difference in how soon the person with dementia moved into a care home.
claims.qualifications: Secondary outcome; wide interval, so not evidence of no effect.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: CI 0.58 to 1.35 is compatible with meaningful benefit or harm.

numbers.meaning: intensity ratio for time to care home

claims.claim: A US counselling and support programme for spouse carers was linked with later nursing home placement.
claims.supporting_passage: Patients whose spouses received the intervention experienced a 28.3% reduction in the rate of nursing home placement compared with usual care controls (hazard ratio = 0.717 after covariate adjustment, p = 0.025). The difference in model-predicted median time to placement was 557 days.
claims.pico_timeframe: 406 US spouse carers of people with Alzheimer disease / counselling and support / usual care / time to nursing home placement / long-term
claims.safe_wording: In a US trial of 406 spouse carers, counselling and support was linked with a later move to a nursing home: a model estimated the typical delay at about 18 months (557 days).
claims.qualifications: Randomised, but 557 days is model-predicted and adjusted; different population, era and programme from START, so do not compare the programmes head to head.

numbers.meaning: model-predicted difference in median time to placement

claims.claim: GMC guidance says listening to relatives' or carers' concerns is not a breach of confidentiality.
claims.safe_wording: Do not quote or attribute to GMC; guidance could not be opened (Drive and PubMed searched).

claims.claim: Carers report being refused information on confidentiality grounds.
claims.supporting_passage: the majority (56.3%) of respondents stated that they have specifically encountered difficulties accessing information from the treating mental health team. The main reasons given to them by the mental health team for withholding information include: lack of patient consent (46.2%) and unavailability of a team member (46.2%).
claims.pico_timeframe: 159 carers of people with mental illness, Irish support group, cross-sectional survey
claims.safe_wording: In an Irish survey of 159 carers of people with mental illness, over half had struggled to get information from the care team, and the commonest reason they were given was lack of the patient's consent.
claims.qualifications: Mental health, not older people's services; self-selected sample.

numbers.meaning: of 159 carers reported difficulty accessing information
of those, told lack of patient consent (denominator not stated in abstract)

claims.claim: Care Act 2014 s10(5) requires a carer's assessment to consider whether the carer is able and willing to continue caring.
claims.safe_wording: Omit; legislation not opened and no published paper quoting it found on PubMed (two searches) or in Drive.

claims.claim: Legal or guideline basis for carer emergency planning (Carers (Scotland) Act, NICE NG150) and a named emergency card scheme.
claims.safe_wording: Omit all legal, NICE and scheme claims; write as practical advice only (a one-page plan written in advance and shared), and at most suggest carers can ask about emergency planning when they have a carer's assessment, without saying it is a legal duty.

candidates.reason: All essential claims supported from abstracts; keep programmes separate (different populations and eras), describe START effect as modest, and state care home result as no clear difference with wide uncertainty.
Meta-analysis supports relative reductions only; absolute arm rates not in retrievable text so no N in 100; NICE and Scottish duty unverified.
candidates.revised_angle: State 'about a quarter fewer readmissions over 3 to 6 months (relative)' with the caveat that programmes had several parts; build the handover checklist from components the trials used (written plan, links to services, demonstration and teach-back); drop NICE and Scottish-law clauses.

candidates.reason: GMC wording could not be opened, so the post cannot quote or attribute it.
candidates.revised_angle: Frame as clinical judgement ('We should always listen to carers; listening does not require sharing the patient's information') backed by the Irish survey showing carers are often refused information citing consent; add the patient-side action of asking and recording whom the patient is happy to share with. No GMC citation.

candidates.reason: Essential claim (Care Act s10(5) willingness wording) could not be verified from an opened copy or a published paper quoting it; per editor, replace with C18-22.
No legal, NICE or scheme claims verified; works as practical advice needing no evidence claim.
candidates.revised_angle: Practical advice only: write a one-page emergency plan in advance (needs, medicines, who to call, keys, routine) and share it with named people; no Carers (Scotland) Act, NICE or card scheme mentions.
